He joined the faculty of the [Massachusetts Institute of Technology](/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology "Massachusetts Institute of Technology") in 1981, where he eventually became the Edwin Sibley Webster [professor](/wiki/Professor "Professor") Electrical Engineering and Computer Science Department.[[4]](#cite_note-bio-4) Preceding this, he was associate director and Chief Operating Officer of the [MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory](/wiki/MIT_Computer_Science_and_Artificial_Intelligence_Laboratory "MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory") and principal of the Theory of Computation research group. He lists himself as faculty director of the MIT-Air Force AI Accelerator, which is designed to make fundamental advances in artificial intelligence to improve Department of the Air Force operations while also addressing broader societal needs.[[4]](#cite_note-bio-4)

During the 1980s, Leiserson was on leave from MIT at [Thinking Machines Corporation](/wiki/Thinking_Machines_Corporation "Thinking Machines Corporation"),[[4]](#cite_note-bio-4) where he invented the [fat-tree](/wiki/Fat-tree "Fat-tree") interconnection network, a hardware-universal interconnection network used in many supercomputers, including the [Connection Machine](/wiki/Connection_Machine "Connection Machine") CM5, for which he was network architect.

He helped pioneer the development of VLSI theory, including the [retiming](/wiki/Retiming "Retiming") method of digital optimization with [James B. Saxe](/wiki/James_B._Saxe "James B. Saxe") and [systolic arrays](/wiki/Systolic_array "Systolic array") with [H. T. Kung](/wiki/H._T._Kung "H. T. Kung"). He conceived of the notion of [cache-oblivious algorithms](/wiki/Cache-oblivious_algorithm "Cache-oblivious algorithm"), which are algorithms that have no tuning parameters for cache size or cache-line length, but nevertheless use cache near-optimally.

In the early 1960s, Woodward began work on what was the most complex natural product synthesized to date—[vitamin B12](/wiki/Vitamin_B12 "Vitamin B12"). In a remarkable collaboration with his colleague [Albert Eschenmoser](/wiki/Albert_Eschenmoser "Albert Eschenmoser") in Zurich, a team of almost one hundred students and postdoctoral workers worked for many years on the synthesis of this molecule. The work was finally published in 1973, and it marked a landmark in the history of organic chemistry. The synthesis included almost a hundred steps, and involved the characteristic rigorous planning and analyses that had always characterised Woodward's work. This work, more than any other, convinced organic chemists that the synthesis of any complex substance was possible, given enough time and planning (see also [palytoxin](/wiki/Palytoxin#Total_synthesis "Palytoxin"), synthesized by the research group of [Yoshito Kishi](/wiki/Yoshito_Kishi "Yoshito Kishi"), one of Woodward's postdoctoral students). As of 2019, no other [total synthesis of Vitamin B12](/wiki/Vitamin_B12_total_synthesis "Vitamin B12 total synthesis") has been published.

That same year, based on observations that Woodward had made during the B12 synthesis, he and [Roald Hoffmann](/wiki/Roald_Hoffmann "Roald Hoffmann") devised rules (now called the [Woodward–Hoffmann rules](/wiki/Woodward%E2%80%93Hoffmann_rules "Woodward–Hoffmann rules")) for elucidating the [stereochemistry](/wiki/Stereochemistry "Stereochemistry") of the products of [organic](/wiki/Organic_chemistry "Organic chemistry") [reactions](/wiki/Chemical_reaction "Chemical reaction").[[14]](#cite_note-14) Woodward formulated his ideas (which were based on the [symmetry](/wiki/Symmetry "Symmetry") properties of [molecular orbitals](/wiki/Molecular_orbital "Molecular orbital")) based on his experiences as a synthetic organic chemist; he asked Hoffman to perform theoretical calculations to verify these ideas, which were done using Hoffmann's [Extended Hückel method](/wiki/Extended_H%C3%BCckel_method "Extended Hückel method").
